83d0f55a65b237c8d24f.source: Multiplication by a positive number preserves direction on the number line. Multiplication by a negative number reverses direction. Thus (-2)(3) = -6, (-2)(-3) = 6, and 2(-3) = -6. The rule for two negatives follows from distributivity: 0 = (-2)(3 + (-3)) = -6 + (-2)(-3), so the last product must be 6.

c6dbdbd4fe68f2c5ebb2.source: Subtraction means adding the opposite. For example, 4 - (-5) = 4 + 5 = 9, but -4 - 5 = -9. Parentheses are essential in row operations: if an entry is -5 and you subtract twice a row whose corresponding entry is -3, the new entry is -5 - 2(-3) = 1.

Do not turn the entire expression positive because it contains two minus signs; only the particular subtraction of a negative changes to addition.

265cda8ebb0f14fe9cd4.source: To add fractions, express them with a common denominator. For 1/2 + 1/3, use sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Adding the denominators would produce 2/5, which is a different number. For -3/4 + 5/6, use twelfths: -9/12 + 10/12 = 1/12.

A rounded decimal such as -4.5 is harmless here, but fractions prevent rounding errors from accumulating in longer calculations.

20832f0da7f4e93b752d.source: An expression such as 3x - 2 has a value after x is chosen. An equation such as 3x - 2 = 10 asserts that two expressions have equal values. A solution is a choice that makes the assertion true. Checking x = 4 gives 3(4) - 2 = 10, so 4 is a solution. Checking x = 2 gives 4 rather than 10, so 2 is not.

110b535ac7dc49d68538.source: To solve an equation, preserve its truth by performing the same reversible action on both sides. Starting with 3x - 2 = 10, add 2 to both sides to get 3x = 12; divide both sides by 3 to get x = 4. The phrase 'move -2 to the other side' abbreviates adding 2 to both sides. It is not a separate rule that lets terms cross an equals sign without a reason.

f73174b3bb28bfcc1f54.source: **Worked fraction equation.** Solve x/3 - 2 = 5/6. Add 2 = 12/6 to both sides: x/3 = 17/6. Multiply both sides by 3: x = 17/2. Check: (17/2)/3 - 2 = 17/6 - 12/6 = 5/6. The check uses the original equation and therefore catches a sign error made during rearrangement.

01cc74d4543b8fbc9e80.source: A system asks you to satisfy several equations at the same time. Consider x + y = 5 and x - y = 1. Adding the equations gives 2x = 6, so x = 3. Substitute into the first equation: 3 + y = 5, hence y = 2. Both original equations check: 3 + 2 = 5 and 3 - 2 = 1. Satisfying only the first equation would be insufficient; (1,4) fails the second.

8d36f87f142600c57689.source: If the system instead says x + y = 5 and x + y = 7, subtracting the first equation from the second gives 0 = 2. This cannot be true, so no pair works. If the second equation is 2x + 2y = 10, it repeats the first equation. Every pair (5 - t,t) works, because (5 - t) + t = 5. A repeated equation supplies no new restriction.

f97db1978a22c8ae08a6.source: The graph of an equation is the set of all points satisfying it. For x₂ = 2x₁ + 1, choosing x₁ = 0,1,2 gives points (0,1), (1,3), (2,5). The line passes through all of them. Its slope 2 means a horizontal change of 1 produces a vertical change of 2. A vertical line such as x₁ = 3 cannot be written as x₂ = mx₁ + c, but it is still a linear equation.

788ca55af5cf2e3593c2.source: An equation ax₁ + bx₂ = c with at least one of a,b nonzero describes a line in the plane. Two such lines can intersect once, be distinct and parallel, or coincide. Those pictures correspond to one solution, no solutions, and infinitely many solutions of a two-equation system. Equations in three variables normally describe planes; the common solution must lie in all the specified planes.

535be6df3d522b899064.source: The statement P ⇒ Q means 'if P is true, then Q is true.' It does not automatically assert the reverse. The statement P ⇔ Q means both directions: P implies Q and Q implies P. It is read 'P if and only if Q.' To prove an equivalence, explain both directions or give a chain of already established equivalences.

8221fc2940492d55a19e.source: A universal statement says something about every allowed object. For instance, 'every homogeneous system has a solution' includes systems of every permitted size. One numerical example cannot prove it. The vector x = 0 supplies a solution for an arbitrary matrix A, which is a general argument. A false universal statement can be disproved by a single counterexample satisfying its assumptions and violating its conclusion.

3eb306cc294fbb49b82a.source: A theorem is a mathematical statement proved from definitions and accepted earlier results. Its assumptions matter. 'A consistent system with a free variable has infinitely many solutions' includes the assumption of consistency. Omitting that assumption makes the statement false. A proof is a chain of justified statements that begins with the assumptions and ends with the desired conclusion. An intuitive picture helps explain a theorem, but a proof must cover every case covered by its wording.

A missing variable has coefficient 0. The general form is a₁x₁ + ... + a_n x_n = b, where the coefficients and b are fixed numbers. The unknowns appear to the first power and are not multiplied together.

434503a489c8c2f7ba5b.source: A solution is a list of numbers in the variable order that makes every equation true. The solution set contains every such list. Two systems are equivalent when their solution sets are identical. A consistent system has at least one solution; an inconsistent one has none. A linear system over ℝ has zero, one, or infinitely many solutions. It cannot have exactly two: if p and q are distinct solutions, linearity shows that p + t(q - p) is a solution for every real t.

f17a6d6d4ca8f673bc7f.source: Suppose R and S are two RREF matrices obtained from one matrix. They have the same row span. In an RREF matrix, take any nonzero combination of its nonzero rows, and find the first row in the combination whose weight is nonzero. Its leading pivot is the first nonzero coordinate of the resulting list: all earlier row weights are zero, and all later rows are zero to the left of their own later pivots. Consequently the possible first-nonzero coordinate locations of vectors in the row span are precisely the pivot-column indices. Since R and S have the same row span, they have the same pivot columns, in the same order.

7871926e779407f19508.source: Now compare row i of R with row i of S. Their entries in every common pivot column agree: both have 1 at their own pivot and 0 at the other pivots. Their difference is in the common row span and is zero at every pivot coordinate. But any row combination in R has, in pivot column j, exactly the weight on the corresponding pivot row: the pivot columns are identity columns. If all those coordinates are zero, every row weight is zero, so the entire combination is zero. Thus the difference between the two compared rows must be zero. All corresponding nonzero rows agree, and both matrices place their remaining zero rows at the bottom. Hence R = S. This proves uniqueness while allowing different intermediate operations and different ordinary echelon forms.

but (1,0) is not obtainable from the zero vector.
This counterexample is useful in the course true/false questions.

1333e68730fe91b34b58.source: A one-vector collection {v} is independent exactly when v ≠ 0. If v ≠ 0 and cv = 0, a nonzero entry of v forces c = 0. If v = 0, the coefficient c = 1 gives a nontrivial relation. A collection containing zero is therefore dependent: give zero weight 1 and all others weight 0.

dc561714cd9be91dd74e.source: Two vectors are dependent exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other, including the case where one is zero. To prove independence of two nonzero vectors, show that no single scalar makes all coordinates match. Comparing only one coordinate is not enough when it supplies no restriction, such as a coordinate that is zero in both.

48f4646cc4d445b5d103.source: **Theorem (supplied Theorem 8).** More than n vectors in ℝ^n are dependent. Put p > n vectors into an n × p matrix. There can be at most n pivots, so at least one of the p weights is free. The homogeneous system has a nontrivial solution. The converse is false: two vectors in ℝ^3 may already be dependent, for example (1,0,0) and (2,0,0).

1e58682267c271e6d07a.source: **Definition.** T is linear if T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) for every pair of domain vectors and T(cu) = cT(u) for every domain vector u and every real scalar c. The first property preserves addition; the second preserves scaling. Their combination gives T(cu + dv) = cT(u) + dT(v). This is the superposition principle: a weighted combination of inputs produces the same weighted combination of outputs.

e1e3254dd8792ce0e510.source: Every matrix transformation is linear because matrix-vector multiplication distributes over addition and scalar multiplication. For example, T(x₁,x₂) = (2x₁ - x₂,3x₂) has matrix [2,-1;0,3]. To prove the statement from the definition, let u = (u₁,u₂), v = (v₁,v₂). Then T(u + v) = (2u₁ + 2v₁ - u₂ - v₂,3u₂ + 3v₂) = T(u) + T(v). Also T(cu) = (2cu₁ - cu₂,3cu₂) = cT(u). Arbitrary letters make the proof cover all inputs.

26759fb07033a494861f.source: The supplied exercises also require rotations. For counterclockwise angle θ, the standard matrix is [cos θ,-sin θ;sin θ,cos θ]. The first column is the rotated unit vector (cos θ,sin θ); the second is its perpendicular companion (-sin θ,cos θ). A clockwise rotation uses negative θ. For θ = π/2 the columns are (0,1) and (-1,0); for θ = π they are (-1,0) and (0,-1). Angles in the course exercises are in radians: π radians is a half-turn, π/2 a quarter-turn, and 2π a full turn. The values at π/4 use cos(π/4) = sin(π/4) = 1/√2.

17b96e5a92c88b51fd56.source: A mapping T: ℝ^n → ℝ^m is onto ℝ^m if every b in that declared codomain equals T(x) for at least one input x. In matrix language, Ax = b is consistent for every b ∈ ℝ^m. This is equivalent to the columns spanning ℝ^m and to a pivot in every row of A.

For a linear mapping, one-to-one is equivalent to Ax = 0 having only the trivial solution, to independent columns, and to a pivot in every column of A.

491447d53ebb8e3f1e74.source: If A is m × n, a_{ij} is its entry in row i, column j. The column a_j consists of a_{1j},...,a_{mj}. A diagonal entry has matching indices. A diagonal matrix is square and has zero entries off its main diagonal. An identity matrix is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are all 1. A zero matrix can be any size; all its entries are zero.

children.text: A 3 × 5 coefficient matrix records 3 equations in 5 unknowns. The right-hand-side vector b has 3 entries.
There are 3 pivots distributed among 3 rows.
Pivots occupy different rows. Three pivots among three rows therefore give a pivot in every row. There is no unused coefficient row that could turn into 0 = a nonzero constant.
A pivot in every coefficient row means this equation can be solved for every three-entry b.
Five unknowns but only three pivot columns leave two free variables. They can vary independently; the pivot equations determine the other unknowns.
Every b in ℝ³ has a solution. Every such system has infinitely many solutions, with two free parameters; none has a unique solution.

R3.source: **R3.** Three pivots in three rows give a row pivot everywhere. Thus every b ∈ ℝ^3 is attainable. There are five unknowns but only three pivots, leaving two free variables. Since every system is consistent, each has infinitely many solutions, never a unique one.

If (1,0,0) were on the line, its first entry would force the multiplier to 1/2, which would make the second entry 2 rather than 0. It is outside the span.

nodes.title: Count the output equations and input coordinates

children.text: A has 2 rows and 3 columns. It takes a three-entry input and returns a two-entry output.
There is a pivot in each coefficient row. The existence theorem says Ax = b is consistent for every b in ℝ². This is what onto ℝ² means.

nodes.title: Two pivots cannot fill three columns

children.text: One coefficient column is nonpivot. Its input coordinate is free; choosing it determines the remaining basic coordinates.
The map is onto ℝ². Every b has infinitely many inputs, with one free parameter. It is not one-to-one.

A2.source: **A2.** Two row pivots mean onto ℝ^2 and existence for every b. Three columns with two pivots leave a free coordinate. Every b therefore has infinitely many inputs. Onto does not guarantee uniqueness for a rectangular matrix.

children.text: A row runs horizontally, from left to right. A column runs vertically, from top to bottom. Count rows first when writing a size.
Row 1 is (1,2,3). Row 2 is (0,−1,4). Each row has three entries, so there are three columns.
Take row 1 of A and column 1 of x. Pair entries in their original order: multiply the first pair, the second pair, and so on. Then add.
Take row 2 of A and column 1 of x. Pair entries in their original order: multiply the first pair, the second pair, and so on. Then add.

children.label: The result has 2 rows and 1 column.

children.text: The entries of x are weights. Weight 1 multiplies column 1 of A, weight 2 multiplies column 2, and so on. A negative weight reverses the sign of every entry in that column.
Both methods add exactly the same products. The row method groups them by output entry. The column method groups them by input weight. Regrouping a finite sum does not change its value.

nodes.title: Why the row and column methods agree

children.text: Each output entry adds exactly the same three products in both methods. The row method gathers the products for one output entry. The column method first builds each whole weighted column, then adds corresponding entries. Neither method changes the order of the coordinates.

children.text: This identity holds for every s,t. Conversely, the equation forces exactly x₁ = 2s − t, so no solutions are omitted.
All s,t are real. For s = 1,t = 0 the solution is (2,1,0), which is nontrivial because it is not the zero vector.

H1.source: **H1.** Choose x₂ = s and x₃ = t. Then x₁ = 2s - t, so x = s(2,1,0) + t(-1,0,1). Both direction vectors satisfy x₁ - 2x₂ + x₃ = 0. Choosing s = 1,t = 0 gives the nontrivial solution (2,1,0). Conversely, the single equation forces exactly the displayed first coordinate for every pair of free coordinates.

Separate the starting point from the directions

children.text: The cancellation works for every pair of real parameters. Conversely, every solution must have these coordinates.
This plane is H1 shifted by (5,0,0). The directions are unchanged, so the planes are parallel. The new plane does not pass through the origin.

H2.source: **H2.** The equation gives x₁ = 5 + 2s - t, x₂ = s, x₃ = t. Thus x = (5,0,0) + s(2,1,0) + t(-1,0,1). Substitution gives 5 + 2s - t - 2s + t = 5 for arbitrary s,t. The new plane is a translate of H1 by (5,0,0); it is parallel and does not pass through the origin.

nodes.title: Given: two inputs produce the same b

children.text: We must show that their difference produces zero. A homogeneous equation has zero on the right.
A acts on the subtraction coordinate by coordinate.

nodes.title: Use the extra hypothesis if only zero is homogeneous

children.text: Under that hypothesis the difference cannot be any nonzero vector.
The difference p − q is a homogeneous solution. If the homogeneous equation has only zero, any two solutions of Ax = b coincide; every consistent system then has exactly one solution.

H3.source: **H3.** A(p - q) = Ap - Aq = b - b = 0, so the difference is homogeneous. If zero is the only homogeneous solution, p - q = 0, forcing p = q. Thus any consistent system with this coefficient matrix has exactly one solution.

nodes.title: What does a dependence relation ask for?

children.text: Find weights that are not all zero but whose weighted vectors add to zero. A zero weight on one vector is allowed.

nodes.title: Use the fact that the second vector is twice the first

children.text: At least the weights 2 and −1 are nonzero. This is different from choosing all three weights zero, which always works and proves no dependence.
The three vectors are dependent. They also outnumber the 2 entries in each vector, which independently gives the same conclusion.

I1.source: **I1.** There are three vectors in ℝ^2, so dependence follows from the too-many-vectors theorem. More explicitly, 2(1,2) - (2,4) + 0(0,1) = 0. The weights (2,-1,0) are not all zero, so they give a valid dependence relation. Some weights may be zero.

The only zero-producing input is zero, so the given columns are linearly independent.

nodes.title: First claim: take a subset of an independent collection

children.text: Suppose a weighted sum of the subset vectors is zero. Assign weight 0 to every vector omitted from the full collection. The extended sum is still zero.

nodes.title: Apply independence of the full collection

children.text: Its only zero-producing weights are all zero. In particular, the original subset weights must all be zero. That is exactly independence of the subset.

nodes.title: Second claim: enlarge a dependent collection

children.text: Start with its known zero combination whose weights are not all zero. Give each added vector weight 0. The old nonzero weights remain nonzero, and the extended sum is still zero.
Every subset of an independent collection is independent. Every superset of a dependent collection is dependent. The argument uses zero weights to pass between collections without changing the sum.

I3.source: **I3.** Any zero combination of vectors in the subset can be extended to a combination of the full collection by assigning coefficient 0 to every omitted vector. Full independence forces all those coefficients, including the subset coefficients, to zero. For a superset of a dependent collection, extend one known nontrivial relation by assigning zeros to every added vector. It remains nontrivial, proving dependence.

nodes.title: Choose two nonzero vectors on the same line

children.text: The weights 2 and −1 are not both zero.
The statement is false. Excluding the zero vector is necessary for independence, but is not sufficient: nonzero vectors may still repeat a direction.

I4.source: **I4.** Both (1,0) and (2,0) are nonzero, but 2(1,0) - (2,0) = 0 has nonzero weights. Thus excluding zero is necessary for independence but does not guarantee it.

nodes.title: Compute the image of the given input
A preimage is an input giving the requested output
Add the equations to eliminate x₁
Verify the preimage and its uniqueness

children.text: Each input coordinate is fixed by the equations; neither is free. Equivalently, both coefficient columns have pivots.
The image of (3,−1) is (1,−4). The unique input for output (5,1) is (1,2).

T1.source: **T1.** T(3,-1) = (3 - 2,-3 - 1) = (1,-4). To find the input for (5,1), solve x₁ + 2x₂ = 5 and -x₁ + x₂ = 1. Add the equations: 3x₂ = 6, so x₂ = 2 and x₁ = 1. The answer is unique because both input columns have pivots. Check T(1,2) = (5,1).

children.text: A linear map must send the zero input to the zero output. This nonzero output already disproves linearity of S.

nodes.title: Passing the zero test is not enough for Q

children.text: We must also test whether addition is preserved.

nodes.title: Compare the two sides of additivity

children.text: The two outputs differ. One valid failure is enough to disprove a property required for all inputs.
Neither S nor Q is linear. S fails the zero test; Q fails the addition test.

T2.source: **T2.** S is not linear because S(0,0) = (0,3) ≠ 0. Q sends zero to zero, but Q((1,0) + (0,1)) = Q(1,1) = (1,0), whereas Q(1,0) + Q(0,1) = (0,0). It fails preservation of addition and is not linear.

children.text: Linearity allows the same input weights to be used on the output vectors.

nodes.title: Subtract the other image coordinate by coordinate

children.text: Without linearity, knowing only T(u) and T(v) would not determine this image.

T3.source: **T3.** Assuming T is linear, T(2u - v) = 2T(u) - T(v) = (2,4) - (3,-1) = (-1,5). Without linearity, knowledge of only two images would not determine the image of their combination.

nodes.title: Put the two basis images in columns

children.label: Three output coordinates, two input coordinates: size 3 × 2.

nodes.title: Test one-to-one behavior with zero output

children.text: Only the zero input produces zero. Therefore different inputs cannot collide: if Au = Av, then A(u − v) = 0 forces u = v.
Two columns can supply at most two pivots. Three output rows would require three pivots for onto ℝ³.
The first requested output is 0, but these forced input values produce 1. The target is unreachable.
The standard matrix is the displayed 3 × 2 matrix. The map is one-to-one and is not onto ℝ³.

M1.source: **M1.** T(e₁) = (2,1,0), T(e₂) = (1,-1,3), so A = [2,1;1,-1;0,3]. The two columns are independent: the third row of Ax = 0 forces x₂ = 0 and the first then forces x₁ = 0. Therefore T is one-to-one. Two columns provide at most two pivots, so not all three rows can have pivots; T is not onto ℝ^3. For example, (0,0,1) would force x₂ = 1/3, x₁ = 1/3 from the second row, contradicting the first output 0.

children.text: Every output has second coordinate 0, so (0,1) can never occur. Every horizontal output (c,0) occurs by choosing a = −c. Thus the range is exactly the horizontal axis.

nodes.title: Find distinct inputs with the same output

children.text: The second input coordinate is erased. These distinct inputs collide.
The map is neither onto ℝ² nor one-to-one. Its standard matrix is the displayed diagonal matrix.

M2.source: **M2.** The reflection gives (-a,b), then projection gives (-a,0). The standard matrix is [-1,0;0,0]. All horizontal-axis outputs occur by choosing a appropriately; no output with nonzero second coordinate occurs. All inputs with the same a collide regardless of b, so the map is neither onto ℝ^2 nor one-to-one.

children.text: Every two-entry output is reached, but c can be anything. There is a pivot in each row and a free third input.
The output uniquely records both inputs. But any three-entry target with nonzero last coordinate is missed. There is a pivot in each column and no pivot in row 3.
The first matrix is onto ℝ² and not one-to-one. The second is one-to-one into ℝ³ and not onto ℝ³.

M3.source: **M3.** [1,0,0;0,1,0] has a pivot in every row, but column 3 is nonpivot. It maps ℝ^3 onto ℝ^2 with a free third input. The matrix [1,0;0,1;0,0] has pivots in both columns but lacks a third row pivot. It is one-to-one into ℝ^3 and misses every output with nonzero third coordinate.

N3.source: **N3.** Solve Ax = e₃. The last row gives x₃ = 1. The second gives x₂ + 1 = 0, so x₂ = -1. The first gives x₁ - 1 = 0, so x₁ = 1. Therefore the third inverse column is (1,-1,1), agreeing with N2. The equations ensure A times this column equals e₃.

children.text: We want to prove B = C. We may use A⁻¹ because invertibility is an assumption.

nodes.title: Multiply both sides on the left

children.text: B and C are different even though these products are equal. A is not invertible in this counterexample.
An invertible left factor can be canceled. The displayed singular example shows the assumption cannot be omitted.

N4.source: **N4.** Left-multiply AB = AC by A^(-1). Associativity yields (A^(-1)A)B = (A^(-1)A)C, so B = C. If A = [1,0;0,0], B = [0,0;0,1], C = 0, then AB = AC = 0 although B ≠ C. The invertibility hypothesis is essential.

G1.source: **G1.** The equations are x₁ + 2x₂ = 3 and x₂ + x₃ = 2. Let x₂ = t. Then x₁ = 3 - 2t and x₃ = 2 - t, giving x = (3,0,2) + t(-2,1,-1). Substitution gives 3 - 2t + 2t = 3 and t + 2 - t = 2. For the homogeneous system the same reasoning gives x = t(-2,1,-1), and A(-2,1,-1) = 0. The first solution set is a translate of the second. A has a pivot in each of its two rows, so columns span ℝ^2 and T is onto. It has three columns and two pivots, so its columns are dependent and T is not one-to-one.

nodes.title: Record each rule in the correct action order
Solve the output equations to undo the map

children.text: The products can also be checked entry by entry: the off-diagonal cancellations are 2 − 2 and −2 + 2; the diagonal entries are 1.
The composite sends (a,b) to (−b,a + 2b). Its inverse sends (y₁,y₂) to (2y₁ + y₂,−y₁).

G2.source: **G2.** S has matrix [1,2;0,1], and R has matrix [0,-1;1,0]. Apply S first: (a,b) ↦ (a + 2b,b), then R: (-b,a + 2b). The composite matrix is [0,-1;1,2]. At (1,2) the output is (-2,5). To undo it, let (y₁,y₂) = (-b,a + 2b). Then b = -y₁ and a = y₂ + 2y₁. The inverse rule is (2y₁ + y₂,-y₁), with matrix [2,1;-1,0]. Both products with [0,-1;1,2] give I₂, and the inverse sends (-2,5) to (1,2).

children.text: A is 3 × 3, and Ax = b can be solved for every b in ℝ³. We must prove that each solution is unique and that A is invertible.
The all-right-hand-side existence theorem gives a pivot in every coefficient row. Three rows therefore mean three pivots.

nodes.title: Use the fact that A is square

children.text: Those three pivots occupy three different columns. Since there are exactly three columns, every column is a pivot column. There are no free variables.
Consistency is given for every b. With no free variables, each such system has exactly one solution. In RREF every column now has its own leading 1 and zeros elsewhere, so RREF(A) is I₃.
The inverse theorem says a square matrix reducible to I is invertible.
For a 3 × 4 matrix, three row pivots would leave a fourth column without a pivot. Existence would still hold for every three-entry b, but uniqueness would fail.
Every Ax = b has exactly one solution, and A is invertible.

G3.source: **G3.** Solvability for every b gives a pivot in every row. There are three rows, hence three pivots. Since there are also exactly three columns, each column has a pivot, leaving no free variables. Therefore every consistent system has a unique solution. The RREF of a square matrix with pivots in all columns is I₃, so A is row equivalent to I₃ and is invertible by the supplied inverse theorem. Squareness converts every-row pivots into every-column pivots; that step fails for a 3 × 4 matrix.

children.text: We seek three numbers that make both equations true at the same time. At this stage we are changing notation, not finding their values.
The subscripts 1, 2, and 3 are labels distinguishing three unknown values. They are not powers or multiplication instructions.

nodes.title: 3 · Read one coefficient for every variable

children.text: A coefficient is the number multiplying an unknown. The second equation has no x₁ term, so its x₁ coefficient is 0. The term −x₃ means (−1)x₃.

nodes.title: 4 · Build A from the coefficient rows

children.label: A: 2 equations give 2 rows; 3 unknowns give 3 columns.

children.text: Row 1 records the first equation. Row 2 records the second. Keep the variable order x₁,x₂,x₃ in both rows. The constants do not belong in A.

nodes.title: 5 · Put the unknowns in a column

children.text: The unknown vector has size 3 × 1. Its order matches the three columns of A.

nodes.title: 6 · Put the constants in a separate column

children.text: This vector has size 2 × 1. Its entries follow the order of the two equations.
The sizes (2 × 3)(3 × 1) produce a 2 × 1 output, matching b.

nodes.title: 8 · Read the same multiplication by columns

children.text: The first column carries the x₁ coefficients; multiply that entire column by x₁. Do the same for columns 2 and 3, with weights x₂ and x₃. Add matching coordinates.

nodes.title: 9 · Expand the weighted columns to recover the system

children.text: Matching first coordinates gives equation 1. Matching second coordinates gives equation 2. Every entry has returned to its original place.
